rule_broken: Every customer used on a line must exist in the customer master (BSEG.KUNNR -> KNA1.KUNNR)
rule_source: Referential integrity
finding: Customer 0000100999 is used on 3 lines but does not exist in KNA1.
why_it_matters: Without the master record the customer has no name, country, account group or payment terms, and any inner join with KNA1 silently drops these lines.
impact: These 3 lines cannot be assigned to a known customer: balances per customer and their age would leave them out or show them under an unknown customer.
proposed_action: Keep the lines and flag them as orphan customer; do not drop them in joins.

rule_broken: Every account posted in a company code must be configured for it (BSEG.BUKRS+HKONT -> SKB1.BUKRS+SAKNR)
rule_source: Referential integrity
finding: Account 0000800100 (Revenue - services) is posted 2 times in company code 3000 (7,085.42 GBP) but SKB1 has no record of it for that company code; it exists in the other two.
why_it_matters: SKB1 holds the company-level definition of the account (currency, field status, open-item management). Postings to an account that is not defined for the company are inconsistent with the configuration.
impact: Revenue of company 3000 sits on an account with no company-level definition: it would disappear from any report that joins postings with SKB1.
proposed_action: Keep the lines; confirm with the business whether the account is valid for company code 3000.

rule_broken: Receivables are analysed per identifiable customer; the README only defines CPD as a one-time customer
rule_source: Business rule: one entry per identifiable customer (not stated in the README)
finding: 3 customers are one-time accounts (CPD, name 'One-time customer', no Tax ID, city or postal code; countries ES, US, GB); they have 29 BSEG lines (1 credit memo, 14 invoices, 14 payments), 1 of them open: document 1600000006 (type DG, 236.56 credit on the customer, not cleared).
why_it_matters: A one-time account is a generic record shared by many different buyers, so the buyers cannot be told apart, identified by Tax ID or merged. The missing Tax ID is consistent with the account group, but the README does not state it as a rule.
impact: The open item of a generic account would be shown as if it belonged to one customer, although the buyer behind it is unknown.
proposed_action: Model as OneTimeCustomer and report it apart from identifiable customers.

rule_broken: A record flagged for deletion must be handled explicitly: the flag does not block postings (SAP: LOEVM is not SPERR)
rule_source: SAP behaviour (LOEVM is a deletion flag, not a block)
finding: Customer 0000100023 (Harbor Comercial S.A.) is flagged for deletion but has 2 lines in BSEG (2 cleared, 0 open).
why_it_matters: Dropping flagged customers would silently remove real documents that belong to a settled customer.
impact: One invoice and its payment would disappear from payment-time averages if flagged customers are filtered out; no open item is affected.
proposed_action: Keep the history and expose the flag as a property (isDeleted).

rule_broken: A vendor must be a single record: one Tax ID, one master record
rule_source: Business rule: one legal entity, one vendor master record
finding: Vendors 0000200004 and 0000200072 ('Harbor Systems S.L.U.' / 'HARBOR SYSTEMS SLU') share Tax ID A32661340, city and postal code; the names only differ in case and punctuation. Credit amounts: 123,608.18 and 11,712.25 (company code 1000, EUR); lines 16.
why_it_matters: It is the same company registered twice (2019 and 2025), so its spend is split between two entities.
impact: Harbor Systems appears as two smaller vendors instead of one larger one in any ranking or total by vendor.
proposed_action: Unify by Tax ID: one entity with two identifiers.

rule_broken: The vendor analysis covers suppliers that invoice the company (README: LIEF vendor, EMPL employee for travel expenses)
rule_source: README (account group: LIEF vendor, EMPL employee)
finding: 6 vendor records are employees (EMPL; 6 without Tax ID, all with city and postal code). They have 72 lines in BSEG; their expense claims (type KR) add up to 10,847.34 EUR in company 1000, 5,449.96 USD in company 2000, 8,578.84 GBP in company 3000.
why_it_matters: Employees are paid their expense claims through the vendor ledger, with the same document type (KR) as real suppliers, but they are people, not suppliers.
impact: Employee expense claims would be ranked together with supplier invoices in any total by vendor.
proposed_action: Model as Employee, separate from Vendor, and leave them out of supplier totals.

finding: Vendor 0000200018 has documents 1900000083 and 1900000231 (company 1000, type KR) with the same invoice number F2025966/750, the same amount (340.7) and the same invoice date (2025-05-15); they were posted on 2025-05-15 and 2025-05-19; reversed: neither. Both were paid, by separate payments (1500000094 and 1500000095, posted on 2025-07-17 and 2025-07-18).
why_it_matters: Same vendor, same invoice number, amount and date, and no reversal: the invoice was entered twice. This is the check SAP itself uses to detect duplicate invoices.
impact: The invoice is counted twice in the vendor's total and was paid twice.
proposed_action: Mark as a probable duplicate and decide with the business whether to exclude one of them from the vendor total.

rule_broken: A customer invoice number is issued by the company itself and is unique within the company code (BUKRS + XBLNR)
rule_source: Business rule (the company numbers its own invoices; not stated in the README)
finding: Reference 225-11649 (type DR, company 2000) is used by documents 1800000014 and 1800000141, posted on 2025-01-23 and 2025-08-10, for customers 0000100108 and 0000100109 and amounts 8289.71 and 8978.08. Customers and amounts differ, so it is not a duplicate, but one number identifies two invoices.
why_it_matters: The company numbers its own invoices, so a repeated number is a numbering error or a mistake when entering the reference. It cannot identify one invoice.
impact: If XBLNR is used as the invoice identifier in the graph, two different invoices would be merged into one node and their receivables would be mixed.
proposed_action: Identify invoices by BUKRS + BELNR + GJAHR, never by XBLNR; ask the source why the number repeats.

rule_broken: Year and key date are measured on one stated reference date (challenge rule: key date 31 Dec 2025; the date field to use is not specified)
rule_source: Challenge rules (key date) and README (date fields)
finding: 8 documents (type KR, vendor invoices) have a document date in December 2024 and a posting date in 2025. 13 documents posted in December 2025 were entered on 2026-01-01 or 2026-01-02, after the key date; they leave 2 open customer lines and include 1 vendor invoice.
why_it_matters: Three dates describe the same document and fall in different periods for these documents; the date chosen decides which documents belong to 2025 and to the key date.
impact: 8 vendor invoices drop out of 2025 if the document date is used, and 2 open customer lines are missed at the key date if the entry date is used.
proposed_action: State the assumption: use the posting date (BUDAT) for the year and the key date, and the baseline date (ZFBDT) for aging.

rule_broken: A reversed document and its reversal must not be counted in balances or profit and loss
rule_source: SAP behaviour (reversal links STBLG / STJAH)
finding: 14 documents are involved in reversals: 7 reversal documents (type AB, 'Reversal - entry error') and the 7 originals that point to them (40 lines in total). Each original is cleared by its own reversal document, so on its own it still looks like a normal, settled invoice. 2 of the reversals were posted in a later period than their original (company 2000, period 01 to 02; company 3000, period 06 to 07).
why_it_matters: Original and reversal cancel each other. Keeping only the original overstates revenue or cost; keeping only the reversal understates it; both must be treated together.
impact: Including only the originals overstates vendor invoicing, revenue and costs; the clearing date of an original is the reversal date, not a payment, which would distort days-to-pay measures. Where original and reversal fall in different periods, leaving out only one of them moves the amount from one month to another.
proposed_action: Exclude original and reversal from metrics and model the relationship reversedBy.

Each original is cleared by its own reversal document, so on its own it still looks like a normal, settled invoice. 2 of the reversals were posted in a later period than their original (company 2000, period 01 to 02; company 3000, period 06 to 07).
why_it_matters: Original and reversal cancel each other. Keeping only the original overstates revenue or cost; keeping only the reversal understates it; both must be treated together.
impact: Including only the originals overstates vendor invoicing, revenue and costs; the clearing date of an original is the reversal date, not a payment, which would distort days-to-pay measures. Where original and reversal fall in different periods, leaving out only one of them moves the amount from one month to another.
proposed_action: Exclude original and reversal from metrics and model the relationship reversedBy.

rule_broken: Opening balances are not business activity and must be treated apart from the year's postings
rule_source: Business rule: opening balances are not business activity
finding: 3 documents of type SA entered by user MIGRATION on 2025-01-01 ('Opening balances 2025', one per company code): 9 lines, 7 with amounts above 200,000, all on balance-sheet accounts (0 on profit and loss): Bank - main account, Fixed assets - equipment, Retained earnings. 0 lines are on the receivables or payables accounts.
why_it_matters: They carry the balance brought forward, not transactions of the year; mixing them with activity inflates balances and posting counts.
impact: Cash, fixed-asset and equity balances need them; profit and loss is not affected because they only touch balance-sheet accounts. No receivable or payable is brought forward, so every open customer or vendor item comes from a 2025 document.
proposed_action: Exclude from profit and loss; include in balances.

rule_broken: The local amount follows the document amount (DMBTR = WRBTR x BKPF.KURSF); the amounts are positive and the sign comes from SHKZG (README)
rule_source: SAP behaviour (clearing at a different exchange rate)
finding: 36 lines have a document amount of 0 but a local amount: 0000480000 (FX gains): 24, 0000481000 (FX losses): 12. They are exchange-rate differences. Separately, 36 customer/vendor lines in 36 payment documents (EUR, GBP, USD) have a DMBTR that is not WRBTR x KURSF (13 of them by more than 1 %); 36 of those 36 documents contain one of the exchange-rate lines, which carries the difference and balances the document.
why_it_matters: The local amount cannot always be derived from WRBTR x rate; the difference sits on separate exchange-rate lines. SAP produces them when an open item is cleared at a different rate, so the data is correct, but the two columns are not interchangeable.
impact: Summing WRBTR leaves these gains and losses out of profit and loss, and recomputing the local amount as WRBTR x KURSF gives a different figure on the payments settled at another rate.
proposed_action: Use DMBTR as the local-currency amount and never recompute it from WRBTR x KURSF.

rule_broken: A cost center must be valid on the posting date (CSKS.DATAB <= BUDAT <= CSKS.DATBI)
rule_source: Master data validity (CSKS.DATAB / DATBI)
finding: 4 lines were posted to cost center 0000011080 (Store Valencia Centro) between 2025-10-31 and 2025-12-31, after it expired on 2025-06-30 (14,330.05 EUR). In the same company code, cost center 0000011090 (Store Valencia Ruzafa) starts on 2025-07-01.
why_it_matters: The cost center was closed, but postings kept using it. Another cost center with a different name starts the next day; that it replaces the old one is an assumption, the data does not say so.
impact: The old cost center has costs after its end date; if the new one is its replacement, the cost of the store is split between two cost centers.
proposed_action: Keep the postings and expose the validity dates; ask whether they belong to the new cost center.

rule_broken: The payment terms on a customer line normally follow the customer master (BSEG.ZTERM = KNA1.ZTERM)
rule_source: Business rule (not stated in the README)
finding: 11 customer lines have different payment terms from the master, and all of them are credit memos (type DG): the 22 credit memos always carry 0001 on the line, whatever the master says (line 0001 vs master NT30: 4, line 0001 vs master NT60: 7; customers affected: 9). 0 of the 680 invoice lines (type DR) differ from their master.
why_it_matters: A credit memo is posted as due immediately; its terms describe the credit, not a change in what was agreed with the customer. Reading a customer's terms from all of its lines would show two different terms for the same customer.
impact: The terms agreed with these customers look ambiguous if credit memos are included, and the due date of a credit memo is simply its baseline date; 11 of the 11 lines are open items at the key date.
proposed_action: Use the terms on the line to date each item, and take the terms agreed with the customer from the master, which always matches the invoice lines.

rule_broken: A credit memo reduces what the customer owes and is expected to be applied to an invoice or refunded, which clears it
rule_source: Business rule (credit memos reduce receivables; not stated in the README)
finding: 22 of the 22 customer credit memos (type DG) are open at the key date: 6,137.15 EUR in company 1000, 9,002.46 USD in company 2000, 7,084.11 GBP in company 3000. Each one gives in XBLNR the number of the invoice it relates to (22 of 22 match an invoice of the same customer); 19 of those invoices were already cleared by a payment and 3 are still open.
why_it_matters: An open credit memo is a receivable with the opposite sign. Where its invoice was already paid there is nothing left to offset it against, so it is money owed to the customer.
impact: Leaving the credit memos out overstates what customers owe; netting them can leave a customer with a negative balance; and a credit has no meaningful debt age, because it is due on its baseline date.
proposed_action: Keep them as open items with the opposite sign, net them in the customer's balance, show them apart from the age buckets and link each one to its invoice through XBLNR.

finding: 22 of the 22 customer credit memos (type DG) are open at the key date: 6,137.15 EUR in company 1000, 9,002.46 USD in company 2000, 7,084.11 GBP in company 3000. Each one gives in XBLNR the number of the invoice it relates to (22 of 22 match an invoice of the same customer); 19 of those invoices were already cleared by a payment and 3 are still open.
why_it_matters: An open credit memo is a receivable with the opposite sign. Where its invoice was already paid there is nothing left to offset it against, so it is money owed to the customer.
impact: Leaving the credit memos out overstates what customers owe; netting them can leave a customer with a negative balance; and a credit has no meaningful debt age, because it is due on its baseline date.
proposed_action: Keep them as open items with the opposite sign, net them in the customer's balance, show them apart from the age buckets and link each one to its invoice through XBLNR.

rule_broken: Figures for the whole group must be in euros, and the challenge provides no euro exchange-rate table: the rates have to be derived from the data and the method explained
rule_source: Challenge rules (no euro exchange-rate table is provided; derive the rates from the data and explain the method)
finding: The extract has no exchange-rate table. Company codes 2000 and 3000 keep their books in USD and GBP: 3160 of 6062 lines have a local amount that is not in euros. The only rates available are the KURSF of 76 foreign-currency documents: USD/EUR (company 2000) is quoted in 11 of 12 months (missing: 01, which can be obtained by crossing through GBP); GBP/EUR (company 3000) is quoted in 11 of 12 months (missing: 08, which can be obtained by crossing through USD). Within one month the rate of a currency pair varies by up to 0.68 %.
why_it_matters: DMBTR is in the currency of each company code, so it is in euros only for company 1000. The rates have to be rebuilt from documents that happened to be posted in a foreign currency, which leaves gaps and several rates for the same month.
impact: Every euro figure for these two company codes depends on a derived rate: it changes with the method chosen (monthly average, rate of the day, cross rate) and is an approximation in the months with no direct quote.
proposed_action: Build a monthly rate table from KURSF (average per month, inverse and cross rates where there is no direct quote), keep the method used for each month, and convert DMBTR with it.
